environment-variable.def: A named value the shell keeps and passes to programs, such as a password or an API key set with `export PEMS_USERNAME=...`. A `.env` file lists them so scripts can load them.
levels: An environment variable is like a sticky note the computer keeps nearby with a secret written on it, like your login name. Any program you run can peek at the sticky note without you having to say the secret out loud every time.

An environment variable is a named piece of information the shell remembers and hands to any program that runs, like a password or a username. You set one with a command such as `export PEMS_USERNAME=kunal`, and after that any script can read `PEMS_USERNAME` without you typing it again. A `.env` file is just a text file listing several of these so a script can load them all at once. They keep secrets out of the code itself.

`export NAME=value` creates an environment variable in the current shell session, and every program launched from that shell inherits it. In the Fremont traffic project, `PEMS_USERNAME` and `PEMS_PASSWORD` are set this way so the collector script can log in to PeMS without the credentials being written in the code. A `.env` file stores these as `NAME=value` lines, and a library like `python-dotenv` reads it into the process's environment at startup. Because `export` only affects the current shell and its children, closing the terminal loses the variable unless it is saved in a startup file or a `.env`.

Environment variables are a key-value store attached to a process, inherited from its parent shell at the moment it is launched, and invisible to processes that start independently, such as ones started by launchd. This makes them the standard way to inject configuration and secrets into a program without hardcoding them, since the same code can read `PEMS_USERNAME` in development, in CI, and in production, each with a different value supplied by the environment. They fail when a value is exported after a long-running process has already started, since that process keeps the environment it was launched with; they also fail silently when a name is misspelled, since an unset variable usually just reads as empty or `None` rather than raising an error. `.env` files solve the reproducibility problem of remembering many exports by hand, but they are not a secrets vault: anyone who can read the file can read the secret, so `.env` belongs in `.gitignore`, never in the repository.

The security tradeoff is real: environment variables are visible to any process running as the same user, readable from `/proc/<pid>/environ` on Linux, and often captured whole in crash reports, container image layers and CI logs, so treating them as a secure secrets channel is a common and costly mistake. The alternative — a credential manager or secret-injection service that hands out short-lived tokens at runtime — avoids leaving a long-lived password sitting in plaintext, at the cost of more moving parts. A subtler bug is precedence: a variable set in the shell, one loaded from `.env`, and one baked into a launchd plist can disagree, and whichever loads last silently wins, which is a frequent source of 'it works in my terminal but not when scheduled' failures. Practitioners also conflate 'exported in this shell' with 'set for this program forever'; a background job launched by cron or launchd does not inherit an interactive shell's exports at all, which is exactly why scheduled jobs need their own explicit environment block.

In production ML systems environment variables scale into whole configuration layers — feature flags, per-region endpoints, model version pins — managed by tools like Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets or a credential vault, which add rotation, auditing and access control that a flat `.env` file cannot. The open problem is provenance: when a training run's result depends on an environment variable's value, that value has to be captured in the experiment record, or the run is not reproducible even with identical code and data. At scale, teams increasingly push toward config-as-code — typed, validated configuration objects checked into version control — precisely to get away from untyped, silently overridable environment state.

vs-code.def: A free code editor. Point it at the venv's Python so it runs and checks code with the right libraries.
levels: VS Code is like a big coloring book for writing computer instructions, where the computer helps you see mistakes by underlining them. You open a project's folder in it and it shows you all your files in one place.

VS Code (Visual Studio Code) is a free program for writing and editing code, with color-coded text and built-in error checking. For Python projects it needs to know which Python to use, so you point it at the project's virtual environment (the venv) instead of some other Python on the computer. It can run scripts, show file changes tracked by git, and open a terminal inside the same window. Most people in the course write every script in it.

VS Code is an editor, not a compiler: it highlights syntax, shows inline errors from a linter, and lets you run or debug a script with a keyboard shortcut, but the actual Python still comes from wherever its interpreter setting points. Command Palette then 'Python: Select Interpreter' picks which Python VS Code uses to run and check code; picking the project's `.venv` instead of a system Python is what makes autocomplete and error-checking match the packages actually installed for this project. Its Source Control panel shows the same staged and unstaged changes as `git status`, just clickable. Extensions add most of the useful behavior: the Python extension for linting and debugging, GitLens for blame and history.

VS Code separates 'editing' from 'running': the editor process renders and lint-checks your code using whatever interpreter and language server you configured, while a run or debug session launches a separate Python process, and a mismatch between the two — editor pointed at system Python, terminal running the venv's Python — produces the confusing symptom of code that runs fine in the terminal but shows phantom import errors in the editor. Its integrated terminal is a real shell, so activating a venv there (`source .venv/bin/activate`) affects only that terminal pane, not the interpreter the editor uses for linting, unless the interpreter setting is separately pointed at the same venv. Workspace settings (`.vscode/settings.json`) can pin the interpreter path per project so the whole team gets the same setup from a fresh clone. Extensions run in their own sandboxed process and can be slow or resource-heavy on large repos, which is the usual cause of a 'VS Code feels laggy' complaint that has nothing to do with the code itself.

The core design tradeoff is VS Code's language-server-protocol architecture: intelligence like autocomplete, go-to-definition and type checking comes from a separate long-running server process (Pylance, for Python) that indexes the project, which gives rich, near-IDE features in a lightweight editor shell but means that a stale or confused index — after a large refactor, or a `.venv` swapped out from under it — silently degrades suggestions rather than erroring, and the fix is usually reloading the window or restarting the language server. Remote development (SSH, containers) runs the whole extension host on the remote machine while the UI stays local, which practitioners get wrong by assuming an extension installed locally is available remotely — extensions install per host. For notebooks, VS Code's Jupyter extension executes cells against a real kernel process, which means kernel state (variables from a previous cell) persists independent of what the editor displays, a common source of 'it works when I re-run everything but not from a fresh restart' bugs.

At scale, teams standardize editor configuration itself — shared `.vscode/settings.json`, devcontainer definitions, recommended-extensions lists — as part of reproducibility, so that 'works in my editor' does not silently depend on personal setup the way an unpinned interpreter or a missing linter config would. The frontier is AI-assisted editing built into the same surface, inline completion and chat against the open files, which raises a genuinely open question for research and production code alike: how much of the editor's suggestion should be trusted without the same review a human-written diff gets. None of this changes the basic contract from the age-5 explanation, it is still an editor pointed at an interpreter, but at scale the pointing has to be declared in a file, not remembered by each engineer.

yaml.def: Other text formats for settings. A launchd plist is XML: keys and values inside angle-bracket tags.
levels: YAML, plist and XML are different ways grown-up computers write down lists of settings, like different handwriting styles for the same shopping list. XML writes each item inside little angle-bracket tags, like `<name>eggs</name>`.

YAML, plist and XML are text formats for storing settings and configuration, not code. YAML uses indentation and colons, like `name: value`, and is common for tools like Docker Compose. A plist ('property list') is Apple's format for settings, and on the Mac it is actually written in XML: every key and value sits inside angle-bracket tags, such as `<key>Label</key><string>traffic-predictor</string>`. All three are just structured text a program reads back in.

YAML represents nested data with indentation and `key: value` pairs, and lists with a leading dash, which makes it readable but sensitive to exact spacing — a tab where a space was expected breaks the file. XML wraps every value in an opening and closing tag, `<key>...</key>`, which is more verbose but unambiguous about where each value starts and ends; a launchd job description is written this way, for example `<key>StartInterval</key><integer>300</integer>` to run something every 300 seconds. A plist can also be stored in a binary form, but the human-edited version is the XML one. Docker Compose files use YAML to describe services, networks and volumes.

These are three serialization formats for the same underlying idea, nested key-value data, with different tradeoffs. YAML is terse and human-friendly but has a notoriously large and ambiguous specification (unquoted `yes`/`no`/`on`/`off` parse as booleans in some parsers), so production tooling increasingly restricts itself to a 'safe' subset. XML is verbose but has strict, well-specified parsing and schema validation, which is why Apple standardized on it for plists: a launchd job file that a system daemon parses benefits from XML's unambiguity more than from YAML's brevity. Malformed indentation in YAML fails at parse time with an error whose line number often points at the wrong place, which is the most common practical complaint from people used to XML's tag-matching or JSON's braces.

The historical throughline is that each format traded human-readability against parsing safety in a different place: JSON kept a small, unambiguous grammar at the cost of no comments and stricter syntax; YAML added human conveniences (comments, anchors and aliases for reuse) that also expanded its attack surface — YAML deserialization vulnerabilities, where a parser turns tagged text into arbitrary objects, have caused real security incidents, which is why libraries expose a `safe_load` that restricts parsing to plain data. XML's schema languages (XSD) let a consumer validate a document's shape before trusting it, a discipline YAML and JSON only get via separate tools such as JSON Schema. Practitioners often get bitten by YAML's type coercion, like a version string `1.0` parsing as a float and losing the trailing zero, and by plist binary-to-XML round-tripping silently reordering keys, both of which argue for treating any of these formats as data to be validated, not trusted by inspection.

At scale, hand-written configuration in any of these formats becomes a liability, so large systems generate it from a typed source of truth (a Python or Starlark config object, a Kubernetes custom resource) and treat the YAML, plist or XML file as a compiled artifact rather than something engineers edit directly, closing the class of bugs where a manually edited config drifts from what the code actually expects. On Apple platforms specifically, most engineers now edit plists through Xcode's property list editor or generate them from build settings rather than hand-writing XML, for the same reason. The open tooling question across the industry is whether a stricter, still human-editable format like TOML or CUE can replace YAML's role without losing its readability advantage.

mainline.def: A detector on the through lanes, as opposed to an on-ramp, off-ramp or HOV lane. The course uses mainline stations only.
levels: Imagine a highway is a big river of cars. A mainline sensor sits in that main river, not on the little ramps where cars join or leave.

PeMS labels every sensor station by type: ML means mainline, a sensor on the regular through lanes of the freeway, as opposed to ramp sensors (on-ramps and off-ramps) or HOV lane sensors. The course only uses mainline stations, filtered with `Type == "ML"`, because they best capture the general flow of traffic rather than the merging behavior at a ramp. A single freeway can have dozens of mainline stations spaced along it.

In the PeMS station metadata, the `Type` column takes values like `ML` (mainline), `OR` (on-ramp), `FR` (off-ramp) and `HV` (HOV lane); `df[df["Type"] == "ML"]` keeps only the through-lane detectors. Mainline stations measure the steady flow of a freeway segment, so they are the natural target for a 'is this segment slow' prediction, whereas a ramp sensor measures something more local, how fast cars are merging or exiting. Ramp metering, a separate traffic-control technique, works by keeping the mainline itself below a breakdown density using ramp signals, which is one reason mainline data specifically matters for congestion prediction.

Restricting to mainline stations is a modeling decision with real consequences: it discards ramp and HOV data that could carry predictive signal, a ramp backing up often precedes mainline slowdowns, in exchange for a simpler, more homogeneous set of stations whose readings mean roughly the same thing station to station. Because mainline stations are placed at fairly regular intervals along a corridor, they also support spatial features like adjacency between neighboring stations, which a sparser or differently-typed set of sensors would complicate. The tradeoff shows up directly in the feature set: dropping ramps means losing an early-warning signal that a spatial or graph model could otherwise exploit.

The mainline-ramp distinction interacts with causality in a way that is easy to get backwards: ramp metering is a control applied to on-ramps specifically to keep mainline density in a stable regime, so a period of unusually smooth mainline flow may partly reflect an intervention upstream rather than natural demand, which matters if the model is later used to reason about what would happen absent metering. HOV lane stations, excluded by the `ML` filter, follow different dynamics entirely, a largely uncongested lane isolated from the general lanes by a barrier or paint, so including them without a separate lane-type feature would inject noise. A subtler issue is that 'mainline' is a label on the physical location of the loop detector, not a guarantee of representativeness; a mainline station right after an off-ramp can look artificially fast because the vehicles that would have congested it just exited.

At the scale of a full urban network, treating each detector type, mainline, ramp, HOV, as a distinct node type in a heterogeneous graph, rather than filtering ramps out entirely, is an active research direction, since ramp behavior is often the earliest observable signal of an incident propagating onto the mainline. Production traffic systems fuse mainline-style fixed-sensor data with probe data from phones, which covers roads with no fixed sensors at all and updates the very question of what counts as 'the mainline reading' for a stretch of freeway. The open engineering problem is sensor reliability at scale: a meaningful fraction of PeMS mainline detectors are miscoded, stuck, or silently down at any given time, and a production pipeline has to detect that automatically rather than trust the `Type` column blindly.

five-minute-row.def: One reading per station per five minutes: 288 per day. The slot is the position in the day, 0 to 287.
levels: Every five minutes, each sensor writes down one new number, like taking a photo of the traffic over and over all day. If you counted all the photos from midnight to midnight, you'd have 288 of them, and each photo's turn in line is called its slot.

PeMS reports traffic data as a five-minute row: one measurement of speed, flow and occupancy per station, every five minutes, all day. Since a day has 24 times 60 divided by 5 equals 288 five-minute periods, each station produces 288 rows a day. The 'slot' is just which of those 288 periods a row belongs to; slot 0 is midnight to 12:05am, slot 287 is the last five minutes before midnight.

A five-minute row has a timestamp, a station id, and measurements like average speed, total flow (vehicle count) and occupancy for that window; `pct_obs` records what fraction of that row came from real detector readings versus PeMS's own imputation. The slot number, computed as `(hour * 60 + minute) // 5`, ranges from 0 to 287 and is useful as a cyclical feature, capturing 'what time of day is this' without the model needing to learn that hour 23 and hour 0 are close together the way raw hour numbers would suggest they are not. `df.groupby("slot")["speed"].mean()` gives the average speed for each five-minute slot across all days, a quick way to see the daily rush-hour pattern.

The five-minute granularity is PeMS's native aggregation window, chosen historically as a balance between storage volume and enough temporal resolution to see congestion build and dissipate; finer data exists at some stations (30-second) but is far less consistently available. Using slot-of-day as a feature assumes the daily pattern is roughly stationary, Tuesday's 8am slot looks like Wednesday's, which holds well for weekdays but breaks on holidays and days with incidents, so a model trained naively on slot alone will systematically mispredict those days. Because slot is cyclical (287 is adjacent to 0), representing it as a plain integer misleads a linear model into treating 0 and 287 as far apart; encoding it with sine and cosine, or as a one-hot or learned embedding, avoids that. Aggregating five-minute rows up to a coarser interval, 15-minute or hourly, trades temporal resolution for less noise, which is a real modeling choice, not just a preprocessing detail.

The five-minute window is itself an aggregation over the raw 30-second detector polls, and how PeMS aggregates, mean speed across vehicles versus a flow-weighted average, and what it does when some 30-second polls are missing, affects the reported value in ways most users never inspect; two agencies computing 'average speed' slightly differently is a known source of PeMS-versus-other-source disagreement. Slot-of-day as a feature interacts badly with daylight saving time transitions and with detector clock drift, both of which shift which slot a given real-world five minutes lands in; a pipeline that is naive about timezone handling can silently misalign a whole day twice a year. Practitioners often treat every slot as equally reliable, but `pct_obs` varies systematically by time of day, overnight slots have sparser real traffic and more imputation, which means the label noise is not uniform across slots either.

Production traffic systems increasingly move away from a single fixed aggregation window, using multi-resolution representations, raw probe pings aggregated to multiple window sizes, so a model can pick up both fast-changing incidents and slow-changing daily patterns from the same pipeline. At Apple Maps scale, the analogous 'slot' concept has to account for regional daylight-saving rules and local holiday calendars automatically, since a single hard-coded slot-of-day feature that assumes one calendar breaks the moment the system serves another country. An open research question is how much the five-minute boundary itself is an artifact of 1990s hardware rather than a physically meaningful timescale for congestion dynamics, and whether learned, data-driven temporal resolutions outperform any fixed aggregation window.

schema.def: The list of a table's columns and their types. Checked before every write.
levels: A schema is like a rulebook for a toy box that says exactly what kinds of toys go in each bin, blocks in this one, cars in that one, so nothing gets put in the wrong place.

A schema is the definition of what columns a table has and what type each one is, for example, `station_id` is a whole number, `speed` is a decimal, `timestamp` is a date and time. Before the traffic pipeline writes new rows to a table, it checks the schema to make sure the new data has the right columns and types. If a column is missing or a number shows up where text was expected, the write should fail loudly instead of silently corrupting the table.

A schema can be enforced by a database (a `CREATE TABLE` statement with typed columns) or checked in code with a library like pandera or pydantic, which validates a DataFrame against a set of rules, column names, types, allowed ranges, before it is trusted downstream. In the traffic project, a schema check might assert that `speed` is a positive float, `station_id` matches a known station, and `timestamp` falls within the expected day, catching a malformed PeMS download before it silently pollutes a month of training data. `df.dtypes` shows pandas's inferred schema for a loaded table, which is worth comparing against what you expected.

Schema checking is the first and cheapest layer of data validation, catching structural problems, wrong column, wrong type, unexpected nulls, before any statistical check runs, and it is cheap precisely because it does not need to know anything about what 'correct' traffic data looks like statistically, only what shape it must have. A rigid schema fails loudly and immediately on a source format change, which is a feature: silent schema drift, a new PeMS export renaming a column, is far more dangerous than a crash, because it can pass silently into training and degrade a model without any error ever being raised. The tradeoff is between a strict schema, which is safer but brittle to legitimate upstream changes, and a loose one, which tolerates change but pushes the burden of catching errors onto later, harder-to-diagnose stages. Nullable columns need explicit schema decisions: is a missing `speed` an error, or an expected and handled case?

Schema evolution, the fact that a schema legitimately changes over time as new fields are added, deprecated or renamed, is a genuinely hard versioning problem: a schema check that is too strict breaks every time the upstream source adds a harmless new column, while one that is too loose, ignoring unknown columns, can hide a real breaking change. Systems like Avro and Protobuf solve this for streaming pipelines with explicit forward- and backward-compatibility rules, a new field must have a default, a removed field must not be reused for something else, a discipline most pandas-based research pipelines skip entirely, which is why schema bugs are disproportionately common in ML code compared to traditional software. Practitioners often check schema once at ingestion and then trust the data through every subsequent transformation, but a join, a reshape, or a type coercion partway through a pipeline can silently violate the original schema's assumptions, a merge introducing unexpected nulls, without tripping any check placed only at the start.

At scale, schema becomes part of a data contract between teams, the table's producer and its consumers agree on a schema and version it explicitly, with automated tests that fail a deploy if a producer's change would break a downstream consumer's schema expectations, which is the industrial answer to the evolution problem above. Streaming systems add the further complication of late and out-of-order data arriving under an old schema after a new one has already shipped, requiring the pipeline to handle multiple schema versions simultaneously rather than assume a clean cutover. The open engineering challenge is making schema contracts cheap enough to write and maintain that teams actually keep them current, rather than letting them rot into documentation nobody trusts, which is the practical failure mode research prototypes rarely encounter but every production pipeline eventually does.

loc.def: Select by label (`.loc[row, column]`) or by position (`.iloc[0]`). Assigning to `.loc[mask, col]` changes only the masked rows.
levels: Imagine a row of numbered mailboxes with names taped on them. `.iloc` finds a mailbox by counting boxes from the start, while `.loc` finds it by reading the name taped on it.

In pandas, `.loc` selects rows and columns of a DataFrame by their labels (the index value and column name), while `.iloc` selects by plain position, counting from 0, no matter what the labels say. `df.loc[5, "speed"]` gets the value in the row labeled 5 and the column named speed; `df.iloc[0, 1]` gets the value in the first row and second column, wherever it is. You can also use a true/false mask with `.loc`, like `df.loc[df["speed"] < 20, "is_slow"] = True`, which changes only the rows where the condition is true.

`.loc[row_label, col_label]` indexes by label and includes both endpoints when given a slice (`.loc[3:5]` returns rows labeled 3, 4 and 5); `.iloc[row_pos, col_pos]` indexes by integer position and excludes the end, like Python slicing (`.iloc[3:5]` returns two rows). The distinction matters most after filtering or sorting, when a DataFrame's index no longer matches row position 0, 1, 2, `.iloc[0]` after a sort gives the first row in the new order, while `.loc[0]` gives whatever row still carries the label 0, which may be somewhere else entirely. Assignment through `.loc` with a boolean mask, `df.loc[df["speed"] < 20, "is_slow"] = 1`, only touches the rows the mask selects and leaves the rest of the column untouched, which is the safe way to conditionally modify a DataFrame in place.

The label-versus-position distinction reflects a deeper design choice in pandas: the index is data, it can be a date, a station id, anything meaningful, that survives operations like filtering and sorting, so `.loc` lets code refer to 'this specific row' stably across transformations, while `.iloc` refers to 'whatever is currently in this position,' which is only stable if nothing has reordered the data since. Chained indexing, like `df[mask]["col"] = value`, is a common and dangerous anti-pattern that pandas warns about because it may operate on a copy rather than the original DataFrame; `df.loc[mask, "col"] = value` avoids the ambiguity by doing the selection and assignment in one call. `.loc` with a boolean mask is also how conditional feature engineering is usually written in this course, for example labeling a row 'slow' relative to a station's own historical median speed. Both accessors raise an error on an out-of-range label or position, rather than silently returning `None`, which is a deliberate fail-loud design.

Performance differs meaningfully at scale: `.iloc` on a default RangeIndex is effectively array indexing and very fast, while `.loc` on a non-unique or unsorted index can force pandas into a linear scan, so a DataFrame with a duplicated or unsorted datetime index used heavily with `.loc` can become a real bottleneck without any error to signal it, profiling, not intuition, is the way to catch this. A subtler correctness issue is that `.loc` with a slice on a sorted index is inclusive of both ends, but on an unsorted index the behavior of a slice is undefined and pandas will raise, which surprises people coming from plain Python slicing habits. Practitioners frequently reset the index after a groupby or filter specifically to get back to a clean integer index where `.iloc` and `.loc` coincide, trading away whatever meaning the previous index carried for positional simplicity. Multi-indexed DataFrames complicate `.loc` further, since a tuple of labels is required per level, and partial indexing silently returns a sub-frame rather than a scalar if not all levels are specified.

At production data-pipeline scale, `.loc`/`.iloc`-style row-and-label semantics generalize to distributed frameworks (Spark, Dask, Polars), each of which makes different tradeoffs about whether a stable row label even exists across a cluster of machines, Spark DataFrames, for instance, have no guaranteed row order or label at all, which is a real behavioral gap when porting research code written against pandas's `.loc` semantics to a production-scale system. Vectorized, label-aware indexing like this is also foundational to how time-series feature pipelines avoid subtle look-ahead bugs: selecting by a timestamp label rather than a row position is what lets code stay correct even as new data is appended in front of or behind existing rows. The open engineering concern is less about `.loc` itself than about teams building brittle pipelines around pandas's positional guarantees that silently stop holding once the same logic is scaled onto a distributed engine.

float32.def: Number types that use 4 bytes and 1 byte instead of 8. Halving or quartering memory with no real loss for speeds and flags.
levels: Numbers can be written in a big fat notebook or a tiny pocket notebook. float32 and int8 are the small pocket notebooks; they hold plenty of room for a speed or a yes-or-no flag without needing the big one.

Computers usually store decimal numbers as float64 (8 bytes) by default, but float32 (4 bytes) holds almost as much precision using half the memory, which is plenty for something like a traffic speed measured to one decimal place. int8 (1 byte) stores small whole numbers, from -128 to 127, which is enough for a flag like 'is this slow: 0 or 1.' Using the smaller types when you can means a big table of traffic data takes up much less room in memory.

float64 gives about 15-17 significant decimal digits of precision; float32 gives about 7, which is far more than a speed measurement (accurate to maybe 1 mph) actually needs, so `df["speed"] = df["speed"].astype("float32")` halves that column's memory with no meaningful loss. int8 covers -128 to 127 and uint8 covers 0 to 255, both a good fit for a boolean-like flag column or a small category code; `df["is_slow"] = df["is_slow"].astype("int8")` quarters the memory of a column that pandas would otherwise store as a 64-bit integer or float by default. `df.memory_usage(deep=True)` shows exactly how much each column costs before and after the conversion.

Choosing a numeric dtype is a real engineering decision, not a formality: with roughly 100 stations times 288 five-minute steps times 365 days, a year of data is about 10.5 million rows, and even five float64 columns would cost around 420 MB in memory, versus 210 MB at float32, a difference that determines whether a full year fits comfortably in memory on a laptop or forces chunked processing. The risk with narrower types is overflow and precision loss: int8 silently wraps around outside its range in some numeric libraries rather than raising, and float32 accumulates more rounding error over long chains of arithmetic, many additions in a rolling sum, for instance, which matters more for training stability than for storing a single sensor reading. GPUs and Apple's Neural Engine are also simply faster at float32, and increasingly float16, than float64, since consumer hardware allocates far more silicon to lower-precision throughput, so the memory savings come with a real speed benefit during training too. Casting should happen deliberately and early, and the resulting dtype should be checked, since an accidental upcast back to float64 during a computation, like a plain Python `+` with a float64 constant, silently undoes the savings.

Mixed-precision training exploits the same idea deliberately at model-training time: keeping master weights in float32 for numerical stability while running the forward and backward pass in float16 or bfloat16 for speed, with a loss-scaling trick to prevent small gradients from underflowing to zero in the lower-precision format, a technique responsible for a large share of the real-world speedups in modern deep learning training. int8 quantization for inference goes further, mapping a trained float model's weights and activations onto 8-bit integers via a learned or calibrated scale factor, trading a small, carefully bounded accuracy loss for large gains in memory and latency, especially on device. Practitioners commonly get float32-versus-float16 numerical stability backwards, assuming any precision loss is negligible; certain operations, softmax over near-equal logits, or a poorly conditioned loss landscape, are precision-sensitive in ways that show up as training divergence rather than a gentle accuracy drop, which is why frameworks keep certain ops in float32 even inside a nominally float16 training run. bfloat16 versus float16 is itself a real tradeoff, bfloat16 keeps float32's exponent range, avoiding overflow, at the cost of fewer mantissa bits, which is why it dominates on TPUs and increasingly on other accelerators for training specifically.

On-device deployment is where dtype choice stops being an optimization and becomes the product constraint: Apple's Neural Engine and Core ML pipeline are built around float16 and int8 execution, and a model that only runs well in float32 may simply not fit an on-device latency or battery budget, which is why quantization-aware training, simulating low-precision arithmetic during training itself rather than quantizing only after the fact, has become standard practice for models shipping to phones. Research on even lower precision, int4, mixed 4-and-8-bit schemes, and structured sparsity combined with quantization, is active because every further bit removed compounds across billions of inferences a day at Apple's scale. The open problem is automating the precision-assignment decision per layer or per tensor, some layers tolerate int8 fine, others need float16 or better, rather than relying on the current mix of hand-tuning and heuristics.

inputs.def: The columns a model reads. Every one must be known at the row's moment.
levels: Inputs are the clues you give a guessing game before someone guesses the answer, like telling a friend the sky is gray and windy before they guess if it will rain.

Inputs, also called features, are the columns of data a model actually looks at to make a prediction, like a station's recent speeds or the time of day. Every input has to be something you would actually know at the moment you want the prediction; you can't use a speed reading from five minutes in the future as an input for predicting right now, because you would not have it yet. Choosing good inputs is a big part of building a model that works.

In scikit-learn code, the inputs are conventionally called `X`, a table where each column is one feature and each row is one example; the target being predicted is `y`. For the Fremont traffic project, typical inputs include a station's own recent speed lags (`speed_lag_0` through `speed_lag_3`), the time-of-day slot, and the day of week, all values available at the moment the prediction is made, 30 minutes before the label's time. Using a value that would not actually be available yet, like a future speed reading, is called leakage, and it makes a model look far better in testing than it will in real use.

The defining constraint on a valid input is temporal: every feature must be computable using only information available at or before the prediction timestamp, which is a stricter requirement than merely 'the column exists in the training table,' since a table built after the fact can easily contain columns that encode future information without it being obvious from the column name. Feature selection trades off two failure modes: too few inputs and the model cannot express the true relationship (underfitting), too many redundant or noisy inputs and the model can fit spurious patterns in the training set that do not generalize (overfitting), especially with a small amount of training data relative to the number of features. Inputs also need consistent preprocessing between training and prediction time; if speed is standardized using the training set's mean and standard deviation, the exact same values must be used at prediction time, not values recomputed from whatever data happens to be available then. Categorical inputs like station id need an explicit encoding, one-hot, embedding, or a numeric code, before most models can use them at all.

Feature leakage is subtler than 'don't use the future': target leakage occurs when a feature is a proxy for the label computed slightly differently, for example, a rolling average of speed that happens to include the label window's own timestamp due to an off-by-one in the window boundary, and it is dangerous precisely because it inflates validation performance without any obvious code smell, the model looks great until deployment. A second subtlety is that inputs available in a research pipeline are not always available in production at the same latency; a feature that depends on a batch job that runs once a day cannot be an input to a model that needs to predict every five minutes, unless the feature is explicitly allowed to be stale. Practitioners often treat feature engineering as separate from model choice, but the right feature set genuinely depends on the model, a linear model needs explicit interaction terms and nonlinear transforms that a tree-based model or neural network can learn on its own from raw inputs. Feature importance, once computed, is also frequently over-interpreted: a feature can look unimportant only because a correlated feature already carries its signal, not because it carries no information at all.

At production scale, feature availability becomes an infrastructure problem as much as a modeling one: a feature store exists specifically to guarantee that the exact computation used to build a training feature is also used, with matching latency guarantees, to serve that feature at prediction time, since training-serving skew, subtly different feature computation between the two, is one of the most common causes of a model that validates well but underperforms in production. Feature engineering research increasingly moves toward learned representations that reduce reliance on hand-designed features, though for well-understood structured problems like traffic, hand-designed lag and time features still tend to outperform learned ones given realistic data volumes. The open frontier is automating leakage detection itself, static and dynamic analysis tools that can flag a feature computed with information not actually available at serving time, since human review alone reliably misses this class of bug at scale.

lag.def: A value from k steps earlier in the same station's series.
levels: A lag is like remembering what you had for lunch yesterday to help guess what you might want to eat today; it's a peek backward in time at the same thing.

A lag feature takes a value from some number of steps earlier in the same time series and uses it as an input right now. `speed_lag_1` at a given time is just that station's speed reading from one five-minute step before; `speed_lag_2` is two steps before, and so on. Lags are useful because traffic right now is usually a lot like traffic a few minutes ago.

In pandas, a lag is built with `.shift(k)`: `df["speed_lag_1"] = df.groupby("station")["speed"].shift(1)` shifts each station's speed series forward by one row, so every row's `speed_lag_1` holds the previous row's speed for that same station. Grouping by station before shifting matters; without it, the last row of one station's data would leak into the first row of the next station's lag. The course typically builds several lags, `speed_lag_0` through `speed_lag_3`, to give the model a short recent history rather than just the single most recent reading.

Lag features are the simplest and often most effective way to give a model access to a time series' own recent history, working for the same reason autoregressive models like ARIMA have worked for decades: traffic speed is highly autocorrelated at short lags, so recent values carry most of the predictive signal for what comes next. A key correctness property is that lag features are stationary by construction, a lag is always relative to 'now,' so it does not drift in absolute value the way a raw calendar feature or a static station attribute might as roadwork or detector recalibration changes conditions over months. The number of lags to include is a real hyperparameter: too few loses information about trend and acceleration, is speed dropping or recovering, too many adds redundant, highly correlated columns that mostly just add noise and computation. `.shift()` introduces `NaN` values at the start of each group's series, which must be dropped or imputed before training, and forgetting to group by station before shifting is one of the most common leakage bugs in this exact project.

Lag features implicitly assume the process is Markovian at the chosen lag depth, that the last k values summarize everything relevant about the recent past, which is a strong and sometimes wrong assumption; a model that also needs to know whether there was an incident 40 minutes ago outside the lag window will not get that from lags alone and needs either more lags or a genuinely different feature, an event indicator. There's a real tension between engineering explicit lag features for a linear model or LightGBM and letting a recurrent or attention-based model learn its own implicit representation of recent history from a raw windowed sequence; the explicit-feature approach is more interpretable and often more sample-efficient with limited data, while the learned approach scales better with more data and can capture longer or more irregular dependencies. Practitioners frequently compute lags per station correctly but then forget the same discipline when they add lags of a different signal, nearby stations' speeds, say, producing subtle cross-station leakage that is much harder to spot than the single-station case. A related trap is defining a lag relative to a resampled or reindexed series that has silently introduced gaps, which shifts every subsequent lag by an unnoticed amount.

Production time-series systems generally move beyond a small fixed set of hand-picked lags toward automated windowing, a model or search procedure that selects which lags and window statistics actually help, since at scale, thousands of series, changing over time, manually re-tuning lag depth per series does not survive. Sequence models (RNNs, temporal convolutions, transformers) subsume explicit lag features in principle, learning arbitrary functions of the recent window, but in practice production systems often keep a handful of engineered lags as auxiliary inputs even alongside a sequence model, because they are cheap, robust, and provide a useful inductive bias when training data is limited for a given series. An open question, especially for spatial-temporal problems like traffic, is how to combine per-station lag structure with cross-station graph structure in one architecture without one drowning out the other's signal.

calibration.def: Whether a score of 0.3 really means a 30 percent chance. Checked with a reliability diagram; fixed with isotonic regression.
levels: If a weather app says there's a 30 percent chance of rain, calibration is asking: out of all the times it said that, did it actually rain about 3 times out of 10? A calibrated app tells the truth about its guesses.

A calibrated model's probability outputs mean what they say: among all the times it predicted a 30 percent chance of something, that thing should actually happen about 30 percent of the time. You check this by grouping predictions into bins, all the times the model said 'around 30 percent', and comparing the predicted probability to how often the event actually happened in that bin; that comparison is a reliability diagram. If a model is overconfident or underconfident, a fix like isotonic regression can adjust its raw scores into better-calibrated probabilities.

A reliability diagram bins predictions by predicted probability (0-10 percent, 10-20 percent, and so on) and plots the actual observed frequency of the positive class in each bin against the bin's midpoint; a perfectly calibrated model traces the diagonal line. Many models, especially ones optimized purely for ranking or accuracy, like gradient-boosted trees, produce scores that are useful for ordering examples but are systematically over- or under-confident as literal probabilities. Isotonic regression fits a non-decreasing step function mapping raw scores to calibrated probabilities using a held-out calibration set, and Platt scaling, fitting a logistic regression on top of the raw score, is a simpler, parametric alternative that works better with less calibration data.

Calibration and discrimination, the model's ability to separate positive from negative examples, measured by ROC-AUC or average precision, are different properties, and a model can be excellent at one and poor at the other; a model that perfectly ranks examples but always outputs either 0.05 or 0.95 has fine discrimination and poor calibration if the true rate in a given bin is actually 30 percent. This matters operationally whenever a probability is used for a downstream decision that depends on its literal value, setting an alert threshold, combining scores from multiple models, or estimating expected cost, rather than just for ranking or picking the single most likely class. Logistic regression, trained by minimizing log loss, is calibrated 'for free' on data similar to its training distribution because log loss is a proper scoring rule that rewards honest probabilities; tree ensembles and neural networks trained with the same loss can still end up miscalibrated in practice due to overfitting or class imbalance. Calibration must be fit and evaluated on a held-out set distinct from both training and final test data, or the calibration mapping itself will overfit and the reported calibration will be optimistic.

Proper scoring rules give calibration a rigorous foundation: a scoring rule, log loss, Brier score, is proper if the expected score is uniquely minimized by reporting one's true belief, which is why minimizing log loss during training pushes a model toward calibration as a side effect of pursuing accuracy, not as a separate objective, but this guarantee is asymptotic and in-distribution, and it says nothing about calibration under distribution shift or with a misspecified model class. Isotonic regression, being nonparametric, can fit any monotonic miscalibration pattern but needs more calibration data to avoid overfitting the calibration curve itself, especially in low-probability regions where events are rare by definition; Platt scaling's parametric form is more data-efficient but cannot correct a non-sigmoidal miscalibration shape. A common practitioner mistake is calibrating on a random train-test split when the deployment distribution has temporal or spatial shift, a model calibrated on last month's traffic data is not guaranteed calibrated for next month's, especially across a regime change like a new detector coming online. Multi-class and multi-label calibration are considerably harder than the binary case, since fixing marginal calibration per class does not guarantee the joint distribution of predictions is calibrated.

In production ML systems, calibration is often the difference between a model that is merely accurate and one that is safe to act on automatically, a fraud or safety system that fires an automated action at a threshold needs its probabilities to mean what they say, consistently, as the underlying population drifts, which is why production pipelines monitor calibration continuously, not just at launch, and recalibrate on a rolling window. Deep learning models are known to be poorly calibrated by default, especially large, overparameterized networks trained with cross-entropy for many epochs past the point of minimum validation loss, which is why techniques like temperature scaling, a single learned scalar that softens overconfident softmax outputs, are near-universal in production deep learning pipelines. An open research question is calibration under distribution shift and for rare, high-stakes events specifically, where there is not enough data in the tail to verify calibration empirically at all, forcing a choice between trusting an extrapolated calibration curve or falling back to a more conservative, uncalibrated decision rule.

logistic-regression.def: Weighted sum of features plus bias, squashed by the sigmoid into a probability. The simplest model that outputs a probability.
levels: Logistic regression is like a scale that weighs different clues about whether it will rain, adds them up, and then squishes the total into a number between 'definitely not' and 'definitely yes.'

Logistic regression takes each input feature, multiplies it by a learned weight, adds them all up along with one extra number called the bias, and then passes that total through a squashing function called the sigmoid, which turns any number into something between 0 and 1, a probability. It's the simplest model that outputs a real probability instead of just a raw score, which is why it's usually the first model tried on a new problem. Training means finding the weights that make its probabilities match the real outcomes as closely as possible.

The formula is p = sigmoid(w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + ... + b), where the sigmoid function is σ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ), squashing any real number z into the range (0, 1). In scikit-learn, `LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)` finds the weights w and bias b that minimize log loss (also called binary cross-entropy) on the training data, and `.predict_proba(X)` returns the resulting probabilities. For the traffic project, the features might be recent speed lags and time-of-day, and the output is the probability that a station will be slow 30 minutes from now; a threshold, often 0.5, turns that probability into a yes-or-no prediction.

Logistic regression assumes the log-odds of the outcome are a linear function of the features, which is a strong assumption; it cannot represent interactions or nonlinear relationships unless they are added explicitly as extra features, products of existing features, polynomial terms, and it will underfit data with genuinely nonlinear structure. It is trained by maximum likelihood, equivalent to minimizing the cross-entropy loss, using an iterative optimizer, gradient descent or a quasi-Newton method like L-BFGS, since there is no closed-form solution the way there is for plain linear regression. Its main strengths are calibration, its probabilities tend to be honest, since it is optimizing a proper scoring rule directly, and interpretability, each weight says how log-odds change per unit of a standardized feature, holding others fixed, which is why it remains the standard first baseline even in a course that goes on to LightGBM and neural networks. It fails when features are highly correlated (weights become unstable and hard to interpret, though predictions are still reasonable), when the true relationship is strongly nonlinear, or when classes are severely imbalanced without any adjustment to the loss or threshold.

Regularization (L2 by default in scikit-learn, sometimes L1 for sparsity) is not optional in practice; without it, on separable or near-separable data, the unregularized maximum-likelihood weights diverge toward infinity, since the model can always reduce the loss further by pushing decision-boundary-crossing points further into certainty, which is a real numerical failure mode, not just a theoretical curiosity. The decision boundary is linear in feature space, but with sufficient hand-engineered nonlinear features it can approximate more complex boundaries, a fact often used to argue logistic regression is 'inside' every neural network's output layer, since the final layer of a classification network is exactly a logistic or softmax regression on the learned representation beneath it. Practitioners commonly misread the coefficients as measuring 'importance' in an absolute sense, but a coefficient's magnitude is only meaningful after standardizing features to a common scale, and correlated features split their shared signal arbitrarily between their coefficients, which can make a genuinely important feature look weak. Convergence warnings from an iterative solver are frequently ignored, but an unconverged fit gives weights that depend on the optimizer's stopping point rather than a true minimum, which quietly undermines any claims about the fitted coefficients.

At production scale, logistic regression remains heavily used specifically because it is fast to train, fast to serve, well-calibrated, and easy to audit and explain to stakeholders and regulators, properties that often matter more than a small accuracy gain from a more complex model, especially in domains with fairness or interpretability requirements. It also serves as the mandatory baseline in any serious modeling effort: a complex model that cannot beat a well-tuned, well-featured logistic regression by a meaningful margin usually is not worth the added complexity, latency, and maintenance cost in production. Current research directions extend the same linear-plus-link-function idea to online and streaming settings, updating weights incrementally as new traffic data arrives without full retraining, and to federated settings where the training data cannot be centralized at all, both active areas where the simplicity of the base model is precisely the point.

standardization.def: Subtract the training mean and divide by the training standard deviation, per column, so features are on one scale.
levels: Standardization is like turning everyone's height, no matter if it was measured in inches or centimeters, into the same simple scale, so you can compare them fairly.

Standardization rescales each feature column so it has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, by subtracting the column's average and dividing by its standard deviation. This matters because raw features can be on very different scales, a speed might range from 0 to 80, while a flag might be 0 or 1, and some models get confused by that mismatch. `StandardScaler` in scikit-learn does this automatically: `scaler.fit(X_train)` learns the mean and standard deviation from the training data, and `scaler.transform(X)` applies them.

The formula for one value x in a column is z = (x - μ)/σ, where μ and σ are that column's mean and standard deviation computed from the training set only. In scikit-learn, `scaler = StandardScaler(); scaler.fit(X_train); X_train_scaled = scaler.transform(X_train)`, and critically, the same fitted scaler, the same μ and σ from training, is applied to the validation and test sets with `scaler.transform(X_test)`, never refit on them. Logistic regression and neural networks trained with gradient descent typically need standardized inputs to converge well and quickly; tree-based models like LightGBM do not need it at all, since they split on thresholds rather than computing weighted sums.

Standardization exists because gradient-based optimizers move through feature space at a rate governed by each feature's scale, so an unstandardized feature with a much larger range than others dominates the gradient and slows or destabilizes convergence; standardizing puts every feature on comparable footing so a single learning rate works reasonably well across all of them. Fitting the scaler only on the training set and applying it unchanged to validation and test data is essential to avoid leakage, computing statistics from data the model should not have access to yet, even indirectly through preprocessing, inflates validation performance in a way that will not hold up on truly new data. Standardization also changes the interpretation of a linear model's coefficients: after standardizing, each coefficient reflects the change in outcome per one standard deviation of that feature, which puts coefficients on comparable footing for judging relative importance, something raw-scale coefficients cannot do. It is not scale-invariant in the way tree-based splits are, which is exactly why LightGBM does not require it while logistic regression and neural networks do.

In production, the scaler's fitted parameters, μ and σ per feature, are themselves an artifact that must be saved and versioned alongside the model; applying a model to features standardized with a different scaler's statistics, even slightly different ones from a later data snapshot, silently corrupts every prediction without necessarily raising an error, since the resulting values are still plausible numbers. Standardization interacts badly with outliers, since a single extreme value inflates the standard deviation and compresses the standardized range of everything else; robust scaling, using median and interquartile range instead of mean and standard deviation, is the standard fix when outliers are expected and not simply errors to be removed. A subtler issue specific to time series like traffic data is nonstationarity: if the true mean or variance of a feature drifts over months, a seasonal traffic pattern change, a new detector's different noise characteristics, a scaler fit once on old training data becomes progressively less appropriate, and this drift can degrade a model's effective calibration even if its raw weights never change. Categorical and binary features generally should not be standardized the same way as continuous ones, and doing so uniformly across a whole feature matrix is a common, easy-to-miss mistake.

At scale, feature scaling parameters are tracked as part of the same versioned artifact as the model weights in a feature store or model registry, specifically to prevent the training-serving skew described above, since a scaler mismatch is one of the most common and hardest-to-detect classes of production ML bugs, predictions degrade smoothly rather than crashing, so it can go unnoticed for a long time. Modern deep learning architectures increasingly fold normalization into the model itself, batch normalization, layer normalization, rather than relying entirely on a preprocessing step, which shifts some of this burden from a fragile external artifact into a differentiable, jointly-trained component of the network, though even these internal normalization layers carry their own running statistics that must be saved and applied consistently at inference time, so the underlying versioning problem does not fully disappear, it just moves inside the model.

neural-network.def: Layers of weighted sums with a nonlinearity (ReLU) between them. A multilayer perceptron is the plain version.
levels: A neural network is like a row of many tiny logistic-regression helpers stacked on top of each other, each one passing its guess to the next, so together they can notice much more complicated patterns.

A neural network is built from layers, and each layer takes its inputs, computes a weighted sum for several different outputs at once, then applies a nonlinear function, commonly ReLU, which just replaces any negative number with zero, before passing the result to the next layer. A multilayer perceptron, or MLP, is the plainest kind: every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next. Stacking several layers lets the network represent much more complicated patterns than a single logistic regression could, at the cost of needing more data and more computation to train.

Each layer computes h = ReLU(Wx + b), where W is a matrix of weights, x is the input vector, b is a bias vector, and ReLU(z) = max(0, z) is applied to every entry; stacking several such layers, with the last layer using sigmoid or softmax instead of ReLU to output a probability, is a multilayer perceptron. In PyTorch, `nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(10, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 1))` builds a two-layer MLP taking 10 input features to 32 hidden units to a single output. Training uses backpropagation to compute how the loss changes with respect to every weight, and gradient descent to update them; without the ReLU (or another nonlinearity) between layers, stacking linear layers would collapse mathematically into one single linear layer, no more powerful than logistic regression.

The universal approximation theorem says a sufficiently wide single-hidden-layer network can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain arbitrarily closely, which is a statement about representational capacity, not about whether such a network is learnable from finite data with gradient descent; in practice, depth, more layers, each narrower, tends to be a more sample- and parameter-efficient way to reach comparable expressiveness than extreme width. ReLU is preferred over older nonlinearities like sigmoid or tanh in hidden layers largely because its gradient does not vanish for positive inputs, which lets gradients propagate through many layers during backpropagation without shrinking to near zero the way saturating nonlinearities do. An MLP has no structural assumptions about its input, no notion of position, order, or locality, so unlike a convolutional network built for images or a recurrent network built for sequences, it must learn everything about a problem's structure from data alone, which makes it a reasonable default for the traffic project's flat, tabular lag-and-time features but a weak choice for genuinely sequential or spatial structure. Overfitting is a constant risk given enough hidden units and few training examples, addressed with weight decay, dropout, and early stopping on a validation set.

Optimization landscape theory partly explains why heavily overparameterized networks, far more weights than training examples, tend to train reliably despite the loss surface being highly non-convex: results connecting overparameterization to a loss landscape with mostly benign saddle points rather than bad local minima, and the neural tangent kernel perspective viewing very wide networks as approximately linear (kernel) models in weight space, both offer partial explanations, though a full theory of why deep learning generalizes as well as it does empirically is still incomplete. Initialization scheme (Xavier or He initialization, chosen to match ReLU's asymmetry) and learning rate interact nontrivially with depth; too naive an initialization compounds through many layers into vanishing or exploding activations before training even starts, which is why deep MLPs were historically hard to train before these initialization schemes and normalization layers became standard. Practitioners commonly under-tune an MLP baseline, default hidden sizes, no learning-rate schedule, and conclude neural networks 'don't work' on their tabular problem, when in practice a well-tuned gradient-boosted tree often does genuinely outperform a naively-trained MLP on small-to-medium tabular data like PeMS traffic tables, which is a real, empirically-documented finding, not just poor tuning, though the gap narrows with enough data and with modern tabular-specific architectures.

At production and research scale, plain MLPs mostly persist as a component inside larger architectures, the feedforward block in a transformer is an MLP, and the final classification head of nearly every deep vision or graph model is one, rather than as standalone models for anything but genuinely unstructured tabular problems, where gradient-boosted trees still frequently compete with or beat them given realistic data sizes. On device, an MLP's simplicity, dense matrix multiplies, no exotic ops, makes it easy to run efficiently on the Neural Engine, which matters when the alternative is a more exotic architecture with ops that are poorly supported or slow on mobile silicon. An active research question is when and why depth generalizes better than width holding parameter count fixed, and how that tradeoff shifts as available data and compute both scale up, since the empirical answer keeps changing as larger, better-regularized models are tried.

graph-neural-network.def: A model that lets each station read transformed summaries of its neighbors, using the adjacency matrices.
levels: Imagine every traffic sensor is a kid at a big table who can only whisper to the kids sitting right next to them. After a few rounds of whispering, everyone knows a little bit about what's happening further down the table too.

A graph neural network treats the freeway's stations as nodes in a graph, connected to their physically nearby neighbors by edges, and lets each node update its own representation by combining information from its connected neighbors, this is called neighbor mixing or message passing. Which stations count as neighbors is recorded in an adjacency matrix, a grid of 1s and 0s (or distances) saying which pairs of stations are connected. Doing this once lets a station 'see' its direct neighbors; doing it twice lets it indirectly see its neighbors' neighbors too.

One graph-convolution layer computes something like H' = σ(A · H · W), where A is the (often normalized) adjacency matrix describing which stations connect to which, H is the current matrix of per-station feature vectors, W is a learned weight matrix shared across every station, and σ is a nonlinearity like ReLU, so every station's new representation is a learned, weighted mixture of its own and its neighbors' current representations, the essence of neighbor mixing. Stacking this operation twice lets information reach two hops away, a station's neighbors' neighbors, which for a freeway graph might mean information from a couple of stations up or down the corridor. In the traffic project, this lets a model use the fact that slowdowns tend to propagate upstream from one station to the next, information that a model looking at each station in isolation cannot see.

The adjacency matrix encodes an inductive bias, which relationships the model is told matter before it sees any data, and for road networks it is usually built from physical proximity or direct connectivity, adjacent mainline stations, or stations linked by the same road segment, rather than learned from scratch, since a well-chosen fixed structure both regularizes the model and makes it more sample-efficient than requiring it to discover which stations relate to which. Normalizing the adjacency matrix, row-normalizing, or the symmetric normalization used in the original graph convolutional network paper, prevents high-degree nodes from dominating the aggregation simply by having more neighbors to sum over. A GNN differs from applying the same MLP to every station independently specifically in this neighbor-mixing step; without it, a graph neural network collapses to per-station models that cannot see anything happening a few stations away, no matter how deep the network is. Depth, the number of message-passing layers, trades off receptive field against oversmoothing, too many layers and every node's representation converges toward the same average value across the whole graph, losing the local distinctions that made the graph structure useful in the first place.

Oversmoothing is a well-documented and somewhat surprising failure mode: unlike a plain MLP or CNN, where more layers usually help or at worst plateau, a GNN's performance can degrade past a fairly small number of layers, often just 2 to 4, because repeated neighbor averaging is a low-pass filter on the graph signal, and enough applications of it erase the very local structure the model was meant to exploit, this is a real theoretical result connecting GNN depth to graph Laplacian eigenvalues, not just an empirical curiosity. Static, hand-built adjacency (physical proximity) is a strong prior but misses dynamic relationships, an incident can effectively 'connect' distant stations that share no direct edge by rerouting traffic between them, which motivates attention-based graph models, graph attention networks, that learn edge weights rather than fixing them, at the cost of needing more data and being harder to interpret. Practitioners commonly build the adjacency matrix once from static road geometry and never revisit it, but detector outages, lane closures and construction change which stations are actually informative neighbors of which, a form of structural nonstationarity that a fixed graph cannot represent. For spatio-temporal traffic forecasting specifically, architectures like DCRNN and STGCN interleave graph-convolution layers, spatial mixing, with recurrent or temporal-convolution layers, temporal mixing, and getting the order and balance of the two right is itself an open design question, not a solved recipe.

At the scale of a full metropolitan road network, adjacency structure itself becomes a research and engineering problem: whether to use physical road topology, historical correlation between stations, or a learned graph structure entirely, graph structure learning, inferring edges from data rather than assuming them, and how to keep that structure current as road infrastructure changes without retraining from scratch. Production traffic and mapping systems at Apple's scale combine graph-structured fixed-sensor models with far denser probe data from phones, which effectively supplies a much richer, continuously updated graph signal than any fixed sensor network alone, changing which parts of the GNN framework, fixed adjacency, sparse nodes, still make sense once far more granular position data is available. An open research direction is scaling message passing efficiently to graphs with millions of nodes, a full national road network, without either prohibitive compute cost or the oversmoothing and information-bottleneck problems that plague naive deep GNNs at that scale.

mean.def: The sum of a set of numbers divided by how many there are; the balance point of the data.
levels: The mean is what you'd get if you took everyone's candy, dumped it all in one pile, and shared it back out equally so each person had the same amount.

The mean, or average, is found by adding up a group of numbers and dividing by how many numbers there are. If four stations report speeds of 60, 55, 50 and 65 mph, the mean is (60+55+50+65)/4, which is 57.5 mph. It's the single number that best represents the whole group if you had to pick just one.

The formula for the mean of n numbers x₁ through xₙ is x̄ = (Σxᵢ)/n, the sum of all values divided by the count. In pandas, `df["speed"].mean()` computes it directly, and `df.groupby("station")["speed"].mean()` computes a separate mean per station. The mean is the value that minimizes the sum of squared distances to every point in the data, which is why it shows up naturally as the target of squared-error loss functions.

The mean is sensitive to outliers, a single station reporting an erroneous speed of 500 mph pulls the mean away from where most of the data actually sits, which is why the median (the middle value) is often reported alongside it for skewed data like traffic speeds, where free-flow and congested speeds can be far apart. The sample mean is also the maximum-likelihood estimate of a Gaussian distribution's location parameter, and by the central limit theorem, the mean of enough independent samples is itself approximately normally distributed regardless of the underlying distribution's shape, which underlies most confidence-interval and hypothesis-testing procedures used to compare, say, average speeds across two time periods. A weighted mean, where some values count more than others, weighting by flow volume rather than treating each five-minute reading equally, for instance, is a natural extension when observations are not all equally reliable or representative. Computing a running or rolling mean over a time series, as with `df["speed"].rolling(12).mean()`, is a common smoothing technique distinct from a single overall mean.

The mean's optimality, minimizing squared error, is exactly what makes it fragile to outliers, since squared error penalizes large deviations disproportionately; robust alternatives, a trimmed mean, Huber loss's implicit weighting, trade a small amount of statistical efficiency on well-behaved data for much better resistance to contamination, a tradeoff worth making explicitly for automatically-collected sensor data prone to occasional bad readings. In a time-series context, the sample mean is only a meaningful summary if the series is stationary; computing 'the mean speed' over a period spanning both a traffic incident and normal conditions conflates two different regimes into a number that describes neither well, which is a subtler version of the same problem as reporting a single national average that hides large regional variation. Practitioners often confuse the sample mean with the population mean it estimates, forgetting that the sample mean itself has a standard error, σ/√n, that shrinks only slowly, as the square root of the sample size, meaning a mean computed from a small window of five-minute readings is considerably noisier than one computed from a full day's worth. PeMS's own reported 'average speed' per five-minute row is itself a mean over the individual vehicle detections within that window, so a downstream mean-of-means calculation inherits and can compound whatever aggregation choices PeMS made upstream.

In production monitoring at scale, a single global mean is rarely the right summary; dashboards track means sliced by many dimensions simultaneously, per route, per time-of-day, per device model, precisely because an aggregate mean can hide a regression that only affects a specific segment, a well-known failure mode sometimes framed as Simpson's paradox when a trend reverses upon slicing. Streaming and distributed systems compute running means incrementally, Welford's algorithm, or approximate sketches for streaming quantiles alongside the mean, because recomputing a mean from scratch over unbounded, continuously arriving data is not feasible, and naive incremental summation accumulates floating-point error that these algorithms are specifically designed to avoid. The open engineering discipline is choosing which mean, over what window, what grouping, what weighting, actually answers the operational question at hand, since 'the average' is underspecified until all three are pinned down.

likelihood.def: How probable observed data is under a model's parameters; higher likelihood means the parameters explain the data better.
levels: Likelihood is like guessing which friend most likely made a mess, based on what the mess actually looks like; some guesses fit the clues better than others.

Likelihood measures how well a particular set of model parameters explains the data you actually observed; if the data you saw would be common under one guess of parameters and rare under another, the first guess has higher likelihood. Training a model often means searching for the parameters that make the observed data as likely as possible, a method called maximum likelihood. It's the flip side of probability: probability asks how likely future data is given fixed parameters, likelihood asks how well fixed data supports different parameter choices.

For a single data point, the likelihood is the probability (or probability density) the model assigns to that point given its parameters, written L(θ; x) = P(x | θ). For a whole dataset of independent points, the likelihood is the product of each point's individual likelihood, L(θ) = Π P(xᵢ | θ), which is why in practice people work with the log-likelihood, Σ log P(xᵢ | θ), turning a product of many small numbers into a sum that is numerically stable to compute. Logistic regression is fit by maximizing exactly this quantity: for each training example, the likelihood is p if the true label is 1 and (1-p) if it's 0, and finding weights that maximize the total log-likelihood is mathematically identical to minimizing binary cross-entropy loss.

Maximum likelihood estimation is the dominant framework for fitting parametric models precisely because, under fairly general conditions, it produces estimators with good asymptotic properties, consistency, converging to the true parameter as data grows, and efficiency, achieving the lowest possible variance among unbiased estimators in the large-sample limit, which is a formal justification for 'just maximize the likelihood' beyond it being an intuitively reasonable thing to do. The negative log-likelihood is the loss function underlying most of standard supervised learning: cross-entropy for classification and mean squared error for regression under a Gaussian noise assumption are both negative log-likelihoods of the appropriate distribution, which is why the same optimization machinery, gradient descent on a smooth loss, applies across seemingly different model types. Likelihood assumes a correctly specified probabilistic model; if the true data-generating process is not in the model's family at all, a linear-Gaussian model applied to data with heavy-tailed noise, maximum likelihood still returns an answer, but its theoretical guarantees weaken or fail. Likelihood is not a probability over parameters and does not integrate to 1 over the parameter space, which is a common conceptual confusion, it only becomes a probability over parameters once combined with a prior via Bayes' rule.

The likelihood principle, that all the information in the data relevant to the parameters is contained in the likelihood function, so two experiments producing proportional likelihoods should lead to the same inference, is philosophically contested precisely because it conflicts with frequentist practices like optional stopping, where the experimental design, not just the observed data, affects a p-value's validity, a genuine and unresolved tension between Bayesian and frequentist statistics. In high-dimensional or small-sample settings, maximum likelihood can overfit badly, since it has no built-in preference for simpler explanations, which is why in practice it is almost always paired with regularization, a penalty term equivalent, from a Bayesian view, to adding a prior and instead maximizing the posterior rather than the raw likelihood. Likelihood ratio tests, comparing the likelihood of a restricted model against a fuller one, underlie a large fraction of classical hypothesis testing and, via Wilks' theorem, connect to a chi-squared distribution asymptotically, giving a principled way to test whether adding a feature meaningfully improves a model's fit rather than just adding noise capacity.
